course.title: Ancient Greek: Foundations
course.description: A beginner's introduction to Ancient Greek, taught entirely in English as a humanities subject: who spoke it, the 24-letter alphabet, how nouns take cases, the definite article, and present-tense verbs. Background and context are drawn from the open article on Ancient Greek in Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). The course closes with the great works of Homer, the tragedians, and Plato that make the language worth learning.

questions.prompt: Ancient Greek was written using which writing system?
questions.explanation: Ancient Greek used its own alphabet of 24 letters, the ancestor of both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets - see 'The Greek alphabet and pronunciation'.

questions.prompt: The Greek word 'logos' survives in English words such as...
questions.explanation: Logos (word, reason) gives the ending -logy and the word logic; Greek roots fill English science vocabulary - see 'Why Ancient Greek still matters'.

questions.prompt: Ancient Greek nouns change their endings to show their job in a sentence. This system of endings is called the system of...
questions.explanation: A noun's case ending marks its role (subject, object, and so on) - see 'Nouns, gender, and the five cases'.

questions.prompt: Which dialect of Ancient Greek was used by Plato and the Athenian playwrights?
questions.explanation: Attic, the dialect of Athens, became the prestige form of classical prose - see 'Why Ancient Greek still matters'.

questions.prompt: Koine Greek is best described as...
options: the common dialect that spread across the Greek-speaking world after Alexander
questions.explanation: Koine means 'common'; it was the shared Greek of the Hellenistic era and of the New Testament.

questions.prompt: The Greek letter alpha corresponds most closely to which English letter?
questions.explanation: Alpha is the first letter and gives the 'a' sound; its name is the first half of the word 'alphabet'.

questions.prompt: Homer is traditionally credited with composing...
questions.explanation: The two great epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, stand at the head of the Greek literary tradition - see 'The great works and why they matter'.

questions.prompt: In the verb 'lyo' (I loose), the ending -o marks the...
questions.explanation: The ending -o marks the first person singular, so lyo means 'I loose' - see 'Verbs, person, number, and the present tense'.

questions.prompt: Ancient Greek word order is relatively free mainly because...
options: the endings show each word's job
questions.explanation: Because case and personal endings carry the grammar, the order of the words can vary without changing the core meaning.

lessons.title: Why Ancient Greek still matters
lessons.grammar_note: Ancient Greek is not one uniform language but a family of dialects; Attic prose and Koine are the two forms most learners meet first.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to say roughly who spoke Ancient Greek and when, name its main dialects, explain the special roles of Attic and Koine, and give several everyday examples of how Greek words still live inside English and the vocabulary of science. Warm-up: before reading on, can you think of three English words that end in '-logy' or begin with 'tele-'? Each one is a small piece of Greek you already carry around. Ancient Greek is one of the best-documented ancient languages, and the article on it in Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia stresses how long and how widely it was used. Starting with the big picture, rather than diving straight into endings, makes the grammar that follows feel like part of a living human story instead of a set of dry tables.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Ancient Greek was spoken around the Aegean Sea and across the wider Greek world for well over a thousand years, roughly from the archaic period into late antiquity. It was never a single uniform tongue. Instead it came in regional dialects, among them Ionic, Doric, Aeolic, and Attic. Attic, the dialect of the city of Athens, became the prestige form of literature and philosophy during the classical period, which is why so much of what we read - Plato, the tragedians, the orators - is in Attic. After the conquests of Alexander the Great, a simplified common dialect called Koine, meaning 'common', spread across the eastern Mediterranean. Koine became the shared language of trade, administration, and later of the Christian New Testament. When people say they are learning 'Ancient Greek', they usually mean classical Attic, with Koine close behind.

sections.heading: Key forms & examples
sections.text: The influence on English is enormous, especially in learned and scientific words. Greek bios (life) and logos (word, study) combine to give biology, literally 'the study of life'. Greek tele (far off) gives telephone and television; grapho (I write) gives graph, paragraph, and photograph; micros (small) and scope (look at) give microscope. Political vocabulary is Greek too: demos (people) plus kratos (power) gives democracy. Even the word 'alphabet' is simply the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta, joined together. Short Greek phrases are already within reach: ho logos (transliterated 'ho logos') means 'the word'; kai (transliterated 'kai') means 'and'; ouk (transliterated 'ouk') means 'not'. Notice that you can recognize the sense of many of these roots even before learning a single rule of grammar, simply because English borrowed them so thoroughly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer these, then check yourself. 1) Which dialect of Ancient Greek is the usual prestige form of classical prose? 2) What does the word 'Koine' literally mean? 3) What two Greek roots make up the word 'biology'? 4) The prefix 'tele-' in 'telephone' comes from a Greek word meaning what? 5) Where does the word 'alphabet' come from? Answers: 1) Attic, the dialect of Athens. 2) it means 'common', the shared dialect that spread after Alexander. 3) bios (life) and logos (study, word). 4) 'far off' or 'at a distance'. 5) from alpha and beta, the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. If you spotted even three of these, you already have a feel for how much Greek hides inside English.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming Ancient Greek was a single standardized language like a modern national tongue - it was really a spread of related dialects, and the one you study depends on the authors you want to read. Mistake: confusing Attic and Koine; Attic is the older classical dialect of Athens, while Koine is the later common form. Mistake: thinking Greek roots in English are rare - they dominate the vocabulary of science, medicine, and politics. Exit ticket: (a) Name one Greek dialect besides Attic. (b) Which dialect became the common language after Alexander? (c) Give one English word built from a Greek root. Answers: for example Ionic, Doric, or Aeolic; Koine; for example biology, telephone, or democracy.

lessons.title: The Greek alphabet, breathings, and accents
lessons.grammar_note: The Greek alphabet has 24 letters; sigma is written as the final form ς only at the end of a word; every word starting with a vowel or rho also carries a breathing mark.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to name all 24 letters of the Greek alphabet in order, give the sound of each, recognize the breathing marks and accents that sit on top of the letters, and read a real Greek word aloud using a reconstructed classical pronunciation. Warm-up: you already know two of the letter names by heart, because they are hiding in the word 'alphabet'. Can you spot them? The Greek alphabet is the direct ancestor of both the Latin alphabet we use for English and the Cyrillic alphabet used for Russian, so many letters will feel familiar, while a handful look or sound surprising. Learning the alphabet first is the single most useful step in beginning Greek, because once you can turn the letters into sounds you can read any word aloud, even one you have never seen, and start noticing Greek roots everywhere.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Here are the 24 letters, each with its name and nearest sound. Α α alpha (a as in father), Β β beta (b), Γ γ gamma (hard g), Δ δ delta (d), Ε ε epsilon (short e), Ζ ζ zeta (zd or z), Η η eta (long e, like the a in 'gate'), Θ θ theta (th as in 'thin'), Ι ι iota (i), Κ κ kappa (k), Λ λ lambda (l), Μ μ mu (m), Ν ν nu (n), Ξ ξ xi (x as in 'box'), Ο ο omicron (short o), Π π pi (p), Ρ ρ rho (rolled r), Σ σ ς sigma (s), Τ τ tau (t), Υ υ upsilon (French u or 'ew'), Φ φ phi (ph, like a strong p), Χ χ chi (ch as in Scottish 'loch'), Ψ ψ psi (ps as in 'lapse'), Ω ω omega (long o). Note the two short and long pairs: epsilon versus eta, and omicron versus omega.

sections.heading: Key forms & examples
sections.text: Let us read real words. λόγος (transliterated 'logos') means 'word, reason' and gives English -logy; sound it out: lambda, omicron, gamma, omicron, sigma. θεός (transliterated 'theos') means 'god'. Watch sigma change shape: in σοφία (transliterated 'sophia', wisdom) it is the ordinary σ, but in λόγος it takes the final form ς at the word's end. Now two more marks, in brief. Every word starting with a vowel or with rho carries a breathing: the rough breathing (a small backward comma) adds an 'h', so ἡμέρα (transliterated 'hemera') means 'day'; the smooth breathing (a forward comma) adds nothing, so ἀγαθός (transliterated 'agathos') means 'good'. Initial rho is always rough, which is why English keeps the 'rh' in 'rhetoric', from ῥήτωρ (transliterated 'rhetor'). Classical Greek also had a pitch accent, printed as the acute, grave, or circumflex; beginners simply read the accented syllable with a light stress, as in LO-gos.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check. 1) How many letters are in the Greek alphabet? 2) Which letter is the long 'e', eta or epsilon? 3) What sound does χ (chi) make? 4) When do you write sigma as ς rather than σ? 5) Which breathing mark adds an 'h' sound? 6) Why does English 'rhetoric' keep an 'h' after the r? Answers: 1) twenty-four. 2) eta is the long e; epsilon is the short e. 3) a rough ch, like the ch in the Scottish word 'loch'. 4) only at the very end of a word; everywhere else use σ. 5) the rough breathing, which looks like a small backward comma. 6) because it comes from Greek rhetor, whose initial rho carried the rough breathing. If you can read θεός and σοφία aloud, you have crossed the hardest early threshold in Greek.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the long and short vowel pairs - eta is long e and epsilon short e, while omega is long o and omicron short o. Mistake: giving gamma a soft 'j' sound; in Ancient Greek it is always a hard g, and before γ, κ, or χ it sounds like 'ng', as in ἄγγελος (transliterated 'angelos', the source of 'angel'). Mistake: forgetting the final sigma ς and writing σ at the end of a word. Mistake: dropping the 'h' on a word with a rough breathing, such as hemera, or adding one where a smooth breathing says not to. Exit ticket: (a) How many letters are in the alphabet? (b) Which letter takes a special form at the end of a word? (c) What does a rough breathing add? Answers: twenty-four; sigma, written ς at the end; an 'h' sound at the start of the word.

lessons.title: Nouns, gender, and the five cases
lessons.grammar_note: Ancient Greek shows a noun's job with its ending, not its position; every noun also has a fixed grammatical gender - masculine, feminine, or neuter.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain what grammatical gender and case mean in Ancient Greek, name the five cases and what each one does, and tell the subject from the object in a simple sentence no matter where the words sit. Warm-up: in English, how do we know that 'the dog bites the man' differs from 'the man bites the dog'? We rely on word order alone. Greek, like Latin before it, does something more flexible: it tags each noun with an ending that announces its role, which lets the words move around for emphasis without ever confusing who did what. Understanding the five cases is the backbone of everything that follows, so this lesson is worth reading slowly and coming back to.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every Greek noun carries three pieces of information: gender (masculine, feminine, or neuter), number (singular or plural), and case (an ending that marks its job). Gender is grammatical, not just natural: logos (word) is masculine, sophia (wisdom) is feminine, and biblion (book) is neuter, simply as a fact of the language. There are five cases. The nominative marks the subject, the doer. The accusative marks the direct object, the thing acted upon. The genitive shows possession or source and means 'of'. The dative marks the indirect object and often means 'to' or 'for', and with prepositions 'in' or 'with'. The vocative is used for directly addressing someone, as in calling out a name. Learn what each case does first, then learn the endings that signal it, and Greek sentences will begin to unlock.

sections.heading: Key forms & examples
sections.text: Take the masculine noun λόγος (word). Its five singular cases run: nominative λόγος (transliterated 'logos', the word as subject), genitive λόγου ('logou', of the word), dative λόγῳ ('logoi', to or for the word), accusative λόγον ('logon', the word as object), vocative λόγε ('loge', O word). A feminine noun such as σοφία (wisdom) runs σοφία, σοφίας, σοφίᾳ, σοφίαν in the same four core cases. A neuter noun such as δῶρον (gift) runs δῶρον, δώρου, δώρῳ, δῶρον - note that for neuters the nominative and accusative are always identical. Now a sentence: ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὸν λόγον λέγει (transliterated 'ho anthropos ton logon legei') means 'the person speaks the word', where anthropos is the nominative subject and ton logon the accusative object. Read the endings first, and the roles become clear.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer or translate, then check. 1) Which case marks the subject of a sentence? 2) Which case marks the direct object? 3) What does the genitive case usually express? 4) Give the gender of logos, sophia, and biblion. 5) In ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὸν λόγον λέγει, which word is the subject? Answers: 1) the nominative. 2) the accusative. 3) possession or source - it corresponds to the English word 'of'. 4) logos is masculine, sophia is feminine, biblion is neuter. 5) ho anthropos, because it carries the nominative, even though you must check the ending rather than the position. If you can name the five cases and say what each does, you have the core idea of Greek noun grammar.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the first noun in a sentence must be the subject - always read the ending, not the position, because Greek word order is flexible. Mistake: treating gender as natural rather than grammatical; biblion (book) is neuter and sophia (wisdom) is feminine as fixed facts, not because of meaning. Mistake: forgetting that neuter nouns have identical nominative and accusative forms, so context and the verb must tell you the role. Exit ticket: (a) Name the five cases. (b) Which case is used to address someone directly? (c) What gender is logos? Answers: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, and vocative; the vocative; masculine.

lessons.title: The definite article and noun declension
lessons.grammar_note: The definite article changes form to match its noun in gender, number, and case, so it is the quickest clue to a noun's grammar; Ancient Greek has no separate word for 'a' or 'an'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to recognize the forms of the Greek definite article 'the', use the article as a signpost to a noun's gender, number, and case, and decline a basic first- and second-declension noun alongside it. Warm-up: in English the little word 'the' never changes, whether we say 'the dog', 'the dogs', or 'to the dog'. In Greek that same word is a hard-working chameleon that shifts shape to agree with its noun, and because it does, it quietly tells you most of what you need to know. There is one more friendly feature here: Ancient Greek has no indefinite article, so there is no separate word for 'a' or 'an' to learn - a bare noun supplies that sense on its own.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The definite article agrees with its noun in gender, number, and case, so learning its forms gives you a template for the endings of whole classes of nouns. In the singular the masculine runs ὁ, τοῦ, τῷ, τόν (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative); the feminine runs ἡ, τῆς, τῇ, τήν; and the neuter runs τό, τοῦ, τῷ, τό. In the plural the masculine runs οἱ, τῶν, τοῖς, τούς; the feminine αἱ, τῶν, ταῖς, τάς; and the neuter τά, τῶν, τοῖς, τά. Notice the patterns: the genitive plural is τῶν for all three genders, and the neuter again shows identical nominative and accusative. Because the article so clearly marks case and gender, Greek readers lean on it constantly - spot the article, and you have already half-parsed the noun that follows.

sections.heading: Key forms & examples
sections.text: Pair the article with nouns. Masculine: ὁ λόγος (the word, subject), τοῦ λόγου (of the word), τῷ λόγῳ (to the word), τὸν λόγον (the word, object); plural οἱ λόγοι, τῶν λόγων, τοῖς λόγοις, τοὺς λόγους. Feminine: ἡ σοφία (the wisdom), τῆς σοφίας, τῇ σοφίᾳ, τὴν σοφίαν. Neuter: τὸ δῶρον (the gift), τοῦ δώρου, τῷ δώρῳ, τὸ δῶρον; plural τὰ δῶρα. A sentence: οἱ ἄνθρωποι τοὺς λόγους ἀκούουσιν (transliterated 'hoi anthropoi tous logous akouousin') means 'the people hear the words', where hoi anthropoi is nominative plural and tous logous accusative plural. Another: τὸ δῶρον τῷ φίλῳ (transliterated 'to doron toi philoi') means 'the gift for the friend', with to doron accusative neuter and toi philoi dative. Let the article flag the case before you even reach the noun.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer or translate, then check. 1) What is the masculine nominative singular of 'the'? 2) What is the feminine nominative singular of 'the'? 3) What is the genitive plural of the article for all three genders? 4) Give 'the gift' as a subject, with its article, using doron. 5) Does Greek have a separate word for 'a' or 'an'? Answers: 1) ὁ (ho). 2) ἡ (he). 3) τῶν (ton), the same for masculine, feminine, and neuter. 4) τὸ δῶρον (to doron), neuter nominative singular. 5) no - there is no indefinite article, so a bare noun can mean 'a gift'. If you can call up ho, he, and to for the three genders, the article will guide you through most sentences.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: ignoring the article and trying to parse the noun on its own - the article is usually the clearest signal of gender and case, so read it first. Mistake: inventing a word for 'a' or 'an'; Greek simply has no indefinite article. Mistake: forgetting that the neuter article and noun share one form for nominative and accusative, so ergon and to doron look the same as subject or object. Mistake: overlooking that the genitive plural article is τῶν for every gender. Exit ticket: (a) Give the three nominative singular forms of 'the'. (b) What is the genitive plural of the article? (c) Does Greek have a word for 'a'? Answers: ho (masculine), he (feminine), to (neuter); ton for all genders; no indefinite article exists.

questions.prompt: How many letters are in the Greek alphabet?
questions.explanation: The Greek alphabet has exactly 24 letters, from alpha to omega - see 'The Greek alphabet and pronunciation'.

questions.prompt: The genitive case in Ancient Greek most often expresses...
questions.explanation: The genitive corresponds to English 'of' and marks possession or source - see 'Nouns, gender, and the five cases'.

questions.prompt: The masculine nominative singular form of the definite article 'the' is...
questions.explanation: The masculine 'the' in the nominative singular is ὁ (ho); ἡ is feminine and τό is neuter.
The ending -eis marks the second person singular, so lyeis means 'you (singular) loose'.

questions.prompt: Which case marks the direct object of a verb?
questions.explanation: The accusative marks the direct object, the thing acted upon - the nominative marks the subject.

questions.prompt: For the neuter noun 'doron' (gift), the nominative and accusative singular forms are...
questions.explanation: Neuter nouns always have the same form in the nominative and accusative, so both are doron.

lessons.title: Verbs, person, number, and the present tense
lessons.grammar_note: A Greek verb's personal ending already names its subject, so a separate pronoun is usually unnecessary; the irregular verb 'to be' must be memorized.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to conjugate a regular Greek verb in the present tense, recognize the six personal endings, conjugate the common irregular verb 'to be', and read a sentence in which the verb ending alone tells you who the subject is. Warm-up: if 'lyo' means 'I loose', what might 'lyousi' mean? The ending holds the clue. This is one of the most empowering steps in beginning Greek, because a single set of endings unlocks a huge family of verbs. Once the endings become automatic, you stop translating word by word and start hearing the person and number directly, much as an English speaker hears tense in a verb without stopping to analyze it. The standard teaching verb is lyo, 'I loose' or 'I release'.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Regular Greek verbs of the common type have a stem to which you add personal endings. Take the verb λύω (to loose). Its present active runs: λύω (I loose), λύεις (you loose), λύει (he, she, or it looses), λύομεν (we loose), λύετε (you all loose), λύουσι (they loose). Those six endings - -o, -eis, -ei, -omen, -ete, -ousi - carry both the person (first, second, third) and the number (singular or plural). The very common verb 'to be' is irregular and simply has to be learned: εἰμί (I am), εἶ (you are), ἐστί (he, she, or it is), ἐσμέν (we are), ἐστέ (you all are), εἰσί (they are). Because the ending already names the subject, Greek often needs no separate word for 'I' or 'we' - the verb says it on its own.

sections.heading: Key forms & examples
sections.text: The full present of λύω, as a table in words: λύω ('lyo', I loose), λύεις ('lyeis', you loose), λύει ('lyei', he or she looses), λύομεν ('lyomen', we loose), λύετε ('lyete', you all loose), λύουσι ('lyousi', they loose). The full present of 'to be': εἰμί ('eimi', I am), εἶ ('ei', you are), ἐστί ('esti', he or she or it is), ἐσμέν ('esmen', we are), ἐστέ ('este', you all are), εἰσί ('eisi', they are). Now sentences. τὸν λόγον λύω (transliterated 'ton logon lyo') means 'I loose the word', with no separate word for 'I' because -o supplies it. ὁ ἄνθρωπος σοφός ἐστιν (transliterated 'ho anthropos sophos estin') means 'the person is wise', where estin links the subject to the adjective. φίλοι ἐσμέν (transliterated 'philoi esmen') means 'we are friends'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Translate or supply the form, then check. 1) Translate 'lyomen'. 2) What ending marks the third person plural, and what does lyousi mean? 3) Give 'you (singular) are', from the verb 'to be'. 4) Translate ho anthropos sophos estin. 5) What does the ending -ei tell you about the subject? 6) Say 'we are friends' using philoi. Answers: 1) 'we loose'. 2) the ending -ousi, and lyousi means 'they loose'. 3) εἶ (ei). 4) 'the person is wise'. 5) that the subject is third person singular - he, she, or it. 6) φίλοι ἐσμέν (philoi esmen). Notice again how the ending, not a separate pronoun, carries the person and number.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding a pronoun that the ending already supplies, or mismatching the ending to the subject - a plural subject needs a plural ending such as -ousi. Mistake: treating 'to be' as regular; its forms (eimi, ei, esti, esmen, este, eisi) are irregular and must be learned by heart. Mistake: confusing the singular and plural endings, for instance writing lyomen (we loose) when you mean lyei (he looses). Mistake: forgetting that esti and the other forms of 'to be' link a subject to a predicate rather than taking a direct object. Exit ticket: (a) What does the ending -omen mean? (b) Give the third person singular of 'to be'. (c) What is the first person singular of lyo? Answers: it means 'we'; esti; lyo.

lessons.title: The great works and why they matter
lessons.grammar_note: To read a simple Greek phrase, find the verb, then the nominative subject, then the accusative object; the endings, not the order, tell you who does what.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to read a few simple Greek words and phrases on your own and to name the great authors and works that make Ancient Greek worth the effort - Homer, the Athenian tragedians, and Plato among them. Warm-up: you can already sound out λόγος and θεός, so you can read more than you might think. This final lesson brings the course full circle. Having learned the alphabet, the cases, the article, and the present tense, you now have enough to recognize the shape of real Greek, and it is worth stepping back to see the literature that two and a half thousand years of readers have prized. The grammar is not an end in itself; it is the doorway into one of the richest libraries humanity has produced.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Greek literature begins at a high point with Homer, whose epics the Iliad and the Odyssey, composed in an older poetic dialect, told of the Trojan War and the long voyage home of Odysseus. In fifth-century Athens the great tragedians - Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides - staged plays such as the Oresteia, Oedipus the King, and Medea, works still performed today. The comic poet Aristophanes mocked the politics of his city. Historians Herodotus and Thucydides more or less invented the writing of history in prose. Above all, for students of the language, stands Plato, whose dialogues record the questioning of Socrates in clear and beautiful Attic prose, making them a favorite first text for readers of classical Greek. Learning the language gives direct access to all of this, unfiltered by translation, which is the real reward behind the grammar.

sections.heading: Key forms & examples
sections.text: Put your new skills to work on short phrases. ὁ ἄνθρωπος (transliterated 'ho anthropos') means 'the person'; ἡ σοφία (transliterated 'he sophia') means 'wisdom'. A famous saying attributed to the philosophical tradition, γνῶθι σεαυτόν (transliterated 'gnothi seauton'), means 'know yourself' and was inscribed at Delphi. The opening idea of one of the most famous texts, ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος (transliterated 'en archei en ho logos'), means 'in the beginning was the word'. Notice ho logos is the nominative subject, en (from the verb 'to be') is the verb, and en archei is a dative phrase meaning 'in the beginning'. Reading method: find the verb first, then the nominative subject, then the accusative object, then fit in the genitive and dative extras. Even at this early stage, real Greek is already partly open to you.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Which two epics are credited to Homer? 2) Name one of the three great Athenian tragedians. 3) Whose dialogues, written in clear Attic, are a favorite first text for Greek learners? 4) What does the phrase gnothi seauton mean? 5) In en archei en ho logos, which word is the subject? Answers: 1) the Iliad and the Odyssey. 2) Aeschylus, Sophocles, or Euripides (any one). 3) Plato, who recorded the conversations of Socrates. 4) 'know yourself'. 5) ho logos, the nominative subject, with en as the verb 'was'. If you can pick the subject out of a real Greek clause by its ending, you have met the central goal of this whole course.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a Greek phrase strictly left to right and assuming the first word must be the subject - find the verb and the nominative first, then let the other endings fall into place. Mistake: thinking Homer wrote in the same Attic dialect as Plato; Homeric epic uses an older poetic blend of dialects. Mistake: imagining that the literature is out of reach for a beginner - start with simple Attic prose, such as Plato or short sayings, and build up. Exit ticket: (a) What is the first thing to find when reading a Greek clause? (b) Name one work by a Greek tragedian. (c) Which author's dialogues make a good first reading text? Answers: the verb; for example the Oresteia, Oedipus the King, or Medea; Plato's.
